source.title: INN: A Method Identifying Clean-annotated Samples via Consistency Effect in Deep Neural Networks
source.authors: Dongha Kim; Yongchan Choi; Kunwoong Kim; Yongdai Kim

record.file_problem: Full paper and supplementary materials are present; no apparent truncation or garbling.
record.tranche_reason: The study measures clean and noisy sample prediction patterns over training and reports that the clean-first memorization pattern may fail on imbalanced data.
record.gate_note: The paper does not report fitting completely random labels, training error on random labels, test error at chance, or training time across label-noise fractions. Its cited descriptions of prior work are not extracted as results. Figure-based AUC and accuracy comparisons for INN and DivideMix are omitted because they measure the proposed noisy-label detection or classifier methods, rather than the claim versions.
record.test_reason: The study reports its own clean/noisy prediction trajectories and explicitly identifies imbalanced settings where clean labels are not consistently learned first, bearing on V6.
record.authors_conclusion: The record accurately describes the consistency-effect finding but omits the main methodological conclusion: INN uses neighborhood prediction differences to identify clean labels more stably than small-loss methods, including under heavy corruption and imbalance, at greater computational cost. The authors also report that clean-first memorization need not hold under class imbalance.
record.recipe_differences: The study uses synthetic and real noisy-label classification settings and measures prediction patterns for clean and noisy examples; it does not reproduce random-label fitting or the original random-label intervention.
record.method_sensitivity: The reported clean-first memorization pattern may fail with imbalanced labels; the neighborhood consistency effect is described as less clear in that setting.

fits_no_version.finding: Mean observed-label predictions at interpolated neighbor inputs remain separated between clean and noisy examples across training epochs.
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: Neighborhood prediction consistency can distinguish clean from noisy labels even after their predictions at training inputs become similar.

record.problems: The paper does not report numeric values for the relevant Figure 2 and Figure 6 patterns in the supplied text. The imbalanced-data finding is qualitative, and the study does not directly measure learning order or fitting error.
record.rows_left_out: Omitted AUC comparisons for INN and small-loss methods, test accuracies for INN+DivideMix, and training-time comparisons: these evaluate the proposed noisy-label methods or classifier performance rather than the claim versions. Locations: Sections 4.2–4.6, Tables 1–3, Tables D.1–D.2, and Tables E.1–E.2.

untested.parts: Completely random labeling, near-zero training error, chance test error, and unchanged architecture and hyperparameters.
Time to fit random versus real labels and convergence speed across corruption fractions.
Fitting shuffled pixels, independently permuted pixels and Gaussian-noise inputs.
Perfect training fit together with steadily increasing test error across corruption fractions from zero to complete corruption.
Whether weight decay, dropout and augmentation prevent random-label fitting, and generalization after removing these regularizers.
Direct identification of shared real-data patterns learned before individual noisy examples; completely random-label training and eventual perfect memorization.

record.verdict_notes: Heavy-noise AUC comparisons evaluate detection performance; the explanation that early learning may cease to favor clean labels is conjectural. They do not independently establish a V6 failure. Reported classifier accuracies and INN execution times do not test V1–V5.

versions.untested_parts: Completely random labels, zero or near-zero training error, chance test error, unchanged architecture and hyperparameters.
Relative training time for fitting random versus true labels and convergence across corruption fractions.
Shuffled, independently permuted, and Gaussian-noise inputs.
Perfect training fit and test error across corruption fractions, including whether remaining signal is captured.
Effects of weight decay, dropout, and data augmentation on random-label fitting or true-label generalization.

The study examines clean versus noisy labels, not completely random labels, and does not directly establish that networks first fit shared real-data patterns and later memorize noisy labels across training.

rows.subject: PreActResNet18 (PRN)
rows.operation_detail: Compared expected prediction values for observed labels of clean and noisy samples across training epochs.

conditions.value: varied; not stated in the supplied text for Figure 2

rows.measure: Expected prediction value for the observed label at each input, Ecor and Einc.
rows.value: The clean/noisy prediction-value difference is large at early epochs and diminishes as training proceeds.
rows.note: The authors call this a typical memorization-effect pattern; the text does not provide numeric values or directly report training error.
rows.check: The reported early clean/noisy prediction gap and its later diminution match V6's learning-order pattern; lack of numerical training-error values does not itself make the effect partial. These are mean observed-label probabilities, not direct measurements of shared-pattern learning or perfect memorization.

source_check.locator_found: Section 3.2, Figure 2 caption and discussion; Section 4.1 architecture details.

rows.subject: PreActResNet18 (PRN)
rows.operation_detail: Compared expected prediction values at interpolated neighbor regions of clean and noisy samples across training epochs.

conditions.value: varied; not stated in the supplied text for Figure 2

rows.measure: Expected prediction value for the observed label at neighbor regions, Ecorᵐ and Eincᵐ.
rows.value: The clean/noisy difference at neighbor regions remains significant regardless of training epoch.
rows.note: The result concerns neighborhood prediction values used for noisy-label identification, not direct measurement of when patterns are learned.
rows.check: Persistent separation at interpolated neighbor inputs measures the proposed consistency effect, not the order in which training examples' real and noisy labels are learned. Remove its V6 link. The authors describe a clear difference but provide no statistical significance test.

rows.subject: PreActResNet18 (PRN)
rows.operation_detail: Compared clean/noisy prediction and loss patterns in an imbalanced two-class noisy-label setting.

conditions.value: (1, 2), (3, 8), (4, 5), and (7, 9); first class treated as majority
all images from first class and 10% randomly sampled images from second class
each sample label flipped with probability 0.3

rows.measure: Whether the model prioritizes memorizing clean-labeled data; score distributions are shown in Figure 6.
rows.value: The model does not always prioritize memorizing clean-labeled data; it may instead memorize data with y = 0. The authors say the consistency effect remains observable, though not clearly, and INN separates clean samples to some extent.
rows.note: The text reports a qualified result across the imbalanced analysis; Figure 6 contains separate class-pair histograms without numeric values in the supplied text.
rows.check: Figure 6 evaluates CE at epoch 10, rather than directly tracing learning order; supplementary Figure C.1 adds epochs 1, 5, 10, 15 and 20. The authors explicitly report that clean-first learning does not always hold and observed label 0 can dominate. Remove the INN performance and neighborhood-consistency statements from this V6 row's value.

relationships.condition: PreActResNet18 trained with standard cross-entropy on CIFAR10 with 30% symmetric label corruption.
relationships.reason: R1 reports a large clean/noisy observed-label prediction gap early in training that diminishes later, consistent with clean labels being learned before noisy labels.
relationships.display_finding: A large early gap between clean and noisy observed-label prediction diminished later in training.
